title: Put a blood-pressure cuff on a mannequin's upper arm: wrap it round, close it over the artery mark, then let go
instruction: Wrap the blood-pressure cuff round the mannequin's left upper arm with its arrow on the marked line and its lower edge 2 to 4 cm above the elbow crease, fasten it, then let go.
context: Nursing assistants (O*NET 31-1131.00; BLS OEWS May 2025: 1,448,910 employed) record vital signs many times a shift (O*NET core task: vital signs "such as temperature, blood pressure, pulse, or respiration rate, as directed by medical or nursing staff"), and every blood-pressure reading starts with fitting the cuff. The cuff is a floppy strap: one hand has to lay its start end on the arm while the other brings the free end round, snug, and presses the hook-and-loop closed with the artery mark over the artery and the lower edge 2-3 cm above the elbow crease.
setup: A display-mannequin left arm lies fixed along x in front of the robot, its axis 100 mm above the table on two grey props: a box under the shoulder end and a foam wedge under the forearm. The upper arm tapers from 55 to 49 mm radius (325 mm round the middle, estimated; measured on the real arm before a trial), its underside 45-51 mm above the table and clear between the props. A dark elbow-crease ring marks x 0.35 m, and a dark 4 mm artery line runs along the top of the upper arm. An adult size-11 cuff (520 x 140 x 3 mm, 0.10 kg, estimated) lies flat on the table across under the arm, skin face up, centred under the upper arm 100 mm above the crease; its start end (grey hook patch on the outer face of the first 220 mm) is on the left-arm side and its free end (loop face on the skin face of the last 100 mm) on the right-arm side. Each 20 mm end piece is propped curled up so a gripper can pinch it (a staging aid: on the real cuff each end piece is folded up about 80 deg by hand and held by one strip of masking tape across the fold on its inner side; a real flat cuff is picked up by its edge). A white ARTERY arrow is printed on the outer face 100 mm from the free end, pointing to the cuff's lower edge. One fixed layout; arms start at the ready pose.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial; the run ends with full credit once 1.0 has held for 1 s. 1.0: the closure is engaged, the cuff goes one full turn round the arm and is snug (no part of it more than 10 mm off the skin, or off the layer under it), the artery arrow faces out and is at most 20 mm (along the skin) from the artery line, the cuff's lower edge is 20 to 40 mm above the elbow crease, and both grippers' tool points and pad tips are at least 3 cm from the cuff. 0.6: engaged and snug, but the arrow or the edge height is out of range or a gripper is still on the cuff. 0.3: one full turn round the arm with no part more than 30 mm off, and not closed or not snug. 0 otherwise. The closure engages only when at least 60 mm of the loop face lies within 6 mm of the hook face and a gripper with closed fingers presses on it (its pad tip within 4 mm of the loop face); a pinched or dragged cuff does not close it. Shortcuts that score 0: doing nothing, sweeping the cuff, lifting and dropping it, half a wrap.
reset_notes: Peel the cuff open, lay it flat across under the arm with the start end on the left-arm side, fold each end piece up about 80 deg and tape the fold (one strip of masking tape on its inner side), and set it 100 mm above the crease.
fidelity: Isaac Sim 6.1 rigid-body simulation (PhysX, 20 Hz control). The cuff is 26 rigid 20 mm segments on weakly sprung hinges (estimated); its end pieces are propped curled as a staging aid, and it starts already passed under the arm. Hook-and-loop is task logic, like the merged contact-gated attachment: pressed onto the hook face it holds every hinge at its angle; a peel over 4 N or shear over 10 N opens it (estimated). Bladder, air and stretch are not modelled.
